title: Best impact-resistant shingles for New Hampshire homes 2026
body_markdown:
**Best overall: Owens Corning Duration FLEX. Best for comparing cold-weather material options: CertainTeed NorthGate ClimateFlex. Best for a conventional architectural look: GAF Timberline AS II.** These are the best impact resistant shingles for New Hampshire homes to shortlist for a homeowner-paid roof replacement in 2026, provided your estimate names the exact product and installation requirements.


**TL;DR**

- Owens Corning Duration FLEX leads this shortlist of best impact resistant shingles for New Hampshire homes.
- CertainTeed NorthGate ClimateFlex deserves consideration when comparing polymer-modified asphalt shingles for a New Hampshire roof replacement.
- GAF Timberline AS II suits homeowners seeking impact-rated architectural shingles with a conventional dimensional appearance.
- Choose the complete installation scope, not an impact rating alone; compare decking, flashing, underlayment and ventilation.


## Why this matters

An impact-resistant shingle is one part of a replacement roof. It does not correct deteriorated decking, poorly detailed flashing or an attic ventilation problem. Paying for a higher-rated material while leaving those issues unresolved misses the point.

[Prescott Roofing](https://prescottroofingnh.com/) handles residential roof replacement for homeowners in Southern New Hampshire and Northern Massachusetts. For your 2026 project, request an inspection and a written scope before choosing a shingle. An inspection request is not a confirmed appointment; confirm the date and access arrangements separately.

**The best shingle choice is the named product your contractor can install correctly within a clearly defined replacement scope.** Use the shortlist below to compare materials, then compare what each contractor actually includes.

## What makes the best impact-resistant shingles?

These criteria matter more than a sample board or an unexplained upgrade on an estimate:

- **Documented impact rating:** Ask for the exact product’s current technical sheet and named test standard. A brand-level claim is not enough.
- **Asphalt formulation:** Polymer-modified asphalt changes material flexibility. That makes the formulation relevant, but it does not replace installation instructions.
- **Installation requirements:** Confirm permitted roof slopes, fastening instructions and temperature-related precautions for the selected product.
- **Complete roof details:** Compare the proposed underlayment, water-protection membrane, flashing, ventilation and deck repairs alongside the shingles.
- **Finished appearance:** Compare actual samples and completed-roof photographs. A small sample cannot show the full pattern across a roof.
- **Written scope:** The estimate should identify the product line, not merely promise an architectural or impact-resistant shingle.

No material wins every category. A strong specification with an unclear installation scope is still an incomplete proposal.

## Impact-resistant shingles at a glance

The products below are architectural asphalt shingles with published UL 2218 Class 4 impact classifications. Confirm the current documentation for the exact product specified in your 2026 proposal; a similar name within the same brand is not interchangeable.

| Shingle | Best for | Standout feature | Key limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Owens Corning Duration FLEX](https://prescottroofingnh.com/blog/best-owens-corning-shingle-series-compared-for-nh-roofs) | Overall starting point | SBS polymer-modified asphalt and Class 4 classification | Product selection still requires a separate review of flashing, decking and ventilation |
| [CertainTeed NorthGate ClimateFlex](https://prescottroofingnh.com/blog/best-certainteed-shingle-lines-for-new-hampshire-homes) | Comparing cold-weather material options | Polymer-modified asphalt and Class 4 classification | Material flexibility does not remove cold-weather installation precautions |
| [GAF Timberline AS II](https://prescottroofingnh.com/blog/best-gaf-shingle-lines-for-nh-roof-replacements) | Conventional architectural appearance | SBS-modified asphalt in an impact-rated architectural shingle | Other Timberline products must be evaluated separately; the family name alone is insufficient |

### What the impact classification actually tells you

UL 2218 is a laboratory impact-resistance test for prepared roof-covering materials. Its Class 4 procedure uses a steel ball approximately 2 inches in diameter dropped from 20 feet. Those dimensions describe a controlled test, not a promise about every real-world impact.

**Class 4 is a material-test classification, not a rating for the entire installed roof.** It does not establish the condition of your decking, the quality of your flashing or the adequacy of your attic ventilation.

Keep impact resistance separate from wind resistance, fire classification and water management. Each addresses a different question. Ask your contractor to explain the documentation behind each claim rather than treating the highest impact class as a complete roof specification.

## 1. Owens Corning Duration FLEX: best overall starting point

Owens Corning Duration FLEX combines an architectural shingle profile with SBS polymer-modified asphalt. SBS is a rubber-like modifier used to change asphalt’s flexibility; the product also carries a published Class 4 impact classification.

Duration FLEX is the default starting point here because it combines the impact classification with a formulation worth evaluating for a New Hampshire replacement. That is a selection recommendation, not a claim that it outperforms every competing shingle in every condition.

**Owens Corning Duration FLEX pros:**

- Its named product line makes an estimate more specific than a generic architectural-shingle allowance.
- SBS modification gives you a concrete material characteristic to compare with standard asphalt formulations.
- Its Class 4 documentation lets you evaluate impact resistance against a defined test rather than a sales description.

**Owens Corning Duration FLEX cons:**

- The impact classification does not tell you whether the contractor will replace questionable flashing or address deck deterioration.
- SBS modification does not waive fastening, sealing or temperature-related installation requirements.

Ask the contractor to identify the matching installation instructions and explain the proposed roof assembly. If the estimate names Duration FLEX but leaves the underlayment, flashing and deck-repair terms blank, resolve those omissions first.

**Best for:** Homeowners who want a clear starting specification for comparing impact-resistant architectural shingles.

**Verdict: Buy Owens Corning Duration FLEX when the written scope supports the material choice; hold an incomplete proposal.**

## 2. CertainTeed NorthGate ClimateFlex: best for material comparison

CertainTeed NorthGate ClimateFlex is a polymer-modified architectural asphalt shingle with a published Class 4 impact classification. It belongs on the shortlist when you want to compare asphalt formulations rather than select by color or manufacturer name alone.

For a Southern New Hampshire homeowner, the useful discussion is how the contractor handles the selected material during installation. A cold-weather product description does not answer questions about storage, handling, fastening or seal activation.

**CertainTeed NorthGate ClimateFlex pros:**

- Polymer modification provides a specific material difference to discuss against a conventional asphalt option.
- Its Class 4 classification supports a like-for-like comparison with other impact-rated shingles.
- The exact product name helps keep contractor proposals aligned during revisions.

**CertainTeed NorthGate ClimateFlex cons:**

- Its formulation does not eliminate weather-related installation precautions.
- An architectural profile still needs a full-roof appearance review; a sample alone does not settle the visual choice.

Ask whether the contractor is proposing NorthGate ClimateFlex specifically. Then ask how installation will follow the current instructions under the conditions expected on your scheduled workday. Keep that answer separate from any general claim about working through New England weather.

**Best for:** Homeowners comparing polymer-modified asphalt options who want a detailed discussion of installation conditions.

**Verdict: Buy CertainTeed NorthGate ClimateFlex when the material and installation plan fit; hold if the proposal relies on cold-weather language without explaining the work.**

## 3. GAF Timberline AS II: best for a conventional architectural look

GAF Timberline AS II is an SBS-modified architectural asphalt shingle with a published Class 4 impact classification. It gives homeowners another impact-rated option within a familiar dimensional shingle format.

The important distinction is the complete product name. Timberline is a broader product family, so an estimate that says only Timberline does not establish that Timberline AS II is being supplied.

**GAF Timberline AS II pros:**

- The architectural format suits homeowners who want a dimensional asphalt-shingle appearance.
- SBS modification gives the product a defined formulation to compare with other shortlisted materials.
- Its Class 4 documentation provides a stated impact-test basis for the comparison.

**GAF Timberline AS II cons:**

- The broader Timberline name can leave a proposal ambiguous unless AS II appears in writing.
- Its impact classification does not establish how roof penetrations, wall intersections or ventilation will be handled.

Review the actual sample alongside your siding, trim and masonry. Then check that the signed proposal and any later material substitution identify the same product. A change within the same manufacturer’s range is still a change that deserves your approval.

**Best for:** Homeowners seeking an impact-rated replacement while retaining a conventional architectural-shingle appearance.

**Verdict: Buy GAF Timberline AS II when the exact product and full replacement scope are documented; skip a brand-only specification.**

## Compare the estimate before choosing the shingle

A Prescott Roofing roof replacement estimate should be evaluated by the same standard as any competing proposal: you need to understand the material, the work and the exclusions before agreeing to proceed. Use this checklist for every 2026 estimate, without assuming that a higher-rated shingle means a more complete job.

- **Tear-off:** Identify which roof coverings will be removed and how disposal is handled. Tear-off means removing the existing roofing rather than installing over it.
- **Deck repairs:** Ask how the exposed wood roof deck will be assessed, documented and repaired with your approval.
- **Water protection:** Identify the underlayment and the locations receiving a self-adhered water-protection membrane.
- **Flashing:** Specify what happens at chimneys, walls, valleys and penetrations. Step flashing consists of individual metal pieces integrated with shingles where a sloped roof meets a wall.
- **Ventilation:** Ask what intake and exhaust conditions the contractor will inspect and what changes the proposal includes.
- **Cleanup:** Define debris removal, protection of the property and the final walkthrough.


![A written roof replacement scope connected to six work categories](https://gwvckixiegkllthleuyt.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/workspace-article-images-public/67c8d83f-aa3f-4c3b-a61f-55220e6b1e93/body-b6e3822c761c09c586705fba75a8b9c4.jpg)

*Compare the full replacement scope before deciding on the shingle.*


Roofing quantities often use squares. One roofing square equals 100 square feet of roof area, but your home’s floor area is not its measured roof area. Slopes, overhangs and roof geometry affect the takeoff, while cutting waste is a separate consideration.

Do not compare proposals by shingle name alone. Ask contractors to separate product differences from scope differences so you can see whether you are choosing a different material or leaving out work.

For a Prescott Roofing roof replacement inspection, describe the project as a homeowner-paid replacement and ask for an explanation of visible conditions, proposed work and exclusions. You should leave the estimate discussion knowing what remains uncertain until tear-off and how additional work would be approved.

Ask for an inspection and a written scope covering shingles, flashing, decking and ventilation.

## How these shingles were ranked

This shortlist prioritizes a documented impact classification, a defined asphalt formulation and a product name that can be written into an estimate. The use-case labels help you organize a contractor discussion; they are not results from a comparative field test.

Owens Corning Duration FLEX is the default starting point, CertainTeed NorthGate ClimateFlex is the material-comparison alternative, and GAF Timberline AS II is the conventional-appearance option. Contractor execution remains a separate decision. No shingle ranking substitutes for inspecting your roof and specifying the work.

## Which impact-resistant shingle should you choose?

**Start with Owens Corning Duration FLEX, then compare a fully specified alternative using the same installation scope.** Keep CertainTeed NorthGate ClimateFlex and GAF Timberline AS II in the discussion when their formulation or appearance better matches your priorities.

For your 2026 replacement, choose the proposal you can explain back in plain language: what comes off, what goes on, which details change and which conditions require approval. If those answers are unclear, pause before signing.

## FAQ


**What's the best impact-resistant shingle for a New Hampshire home?**

Owens Corning Duration FLEX is the default starting point in this shortlist because it combines SBS-modified asphalt with a published Class 4 impact classification. CertainTeed NorthGate ClimateFlex and GAF Timberline AS II are alternatives worth comparing within the same installation scope.

**Does Class 4 mean the entire roof is impact-proof?**

No. Class 4 describes performance under a defined laboratory impact test, not an impact-proof roof. It does not establish the quality of decking, flashing, fastening or ventilation.

**Is a flexible shingle enough for a New Hampshire winter?**

No. A flexible asphalt formulation does not replace correct water protection, flashing, ventilation or installation practices. Ask the contractor how the complete roof assembly addresses your home's conditions.

**Is GAF Timberline the same as Timberline AS II?**

No. Timberline is a broader product family, while Timberline AS II identifies a specific product. Require the complete name in your proposal rather than assuming every Timberline shingle has the same classification.

**Should I replace flashing when I replace my shingles?**

Have the contractor assess each flashing detail and state what will be replaced or retained. The estimate should explain the proposed treatment of walls, chimneys, valleys and penetrations rather than leave flashing unspecified.

**What should I ask Prescott Roofing before requesting a replacement estimate?**

Ask Prescott Roofing to explain the proposed shingle, tear-off scope, deck-repair approval process, flashing and ventilation assessment. Request an inspection first, then confirm the appointment separately.

**Can I compare roof estimates using the shingle name alone?**

No. Match the tear-off, underlayment, flashing, deck-repair terms, ventilation work and cleanup before comparing material choices. Otherwise, different scopes can look like equivalent proposals.


## One last thing

Before signing your 2026 proposal, underline every phrase that leaves a decision open: as needed, existing to remain, or equivalent material. Ask what each phrase means, who decides and how your approval is recorded. **A specific shingle name helps; a specific written scope protects the decision you made.**
